signals.title: Trash Walking
signals.description: Reminder : The Savor of the Month theme for November is BROKEN. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! “The objects people leave behind can serve as unintentional, anonymous portraits.” Recently I was excited to learn that journalist Anna Kodé has a book coming out early next year: Unseen Places: Rediscovering the Art of Observation (Preorder: Bookshop.org | Amazon ) Kodé writes for The New York Times , where I have noticed her work and suspected she must be a TAoN kindred spirit . She has written about bollards (one of my favorite objects !), asked what is the best place to cry in New York City , and organized a history-driven walking tour , among many other things. But Unseen Places takes her interest in the overlooked to a whole other level: In the book she explores non-visual observation (I joke in the TAoN book about licking a building, but she actually does it !); works on slowing down and getting grounded; takes inspiration from Sophie Calle, Yoko Ono , and Georges Perec; experiments with maps and walks; and makes a case that we can all better appreciate everything from the sky to the built environment — even trash! I reached out to Kodé to see if I could convince her to suggest a prompt to TAoN readers. She was game, and had an idea I could not refuse (so to speak). “I have one chapter in the book dedicated entirely to observing trash ,” she explains, “and this is one of the methods I explore in that section.” Here it is: Go on a trash walk. It’s simple: walk around your neighborhood, a local park, your favorite beach or wherever you might be, and pick up pieces of litter left on the ground. You’ll make the area a little bit cleaner with the act, but also, noticing trash can be fascinating . What candy are people consuming? Was that torn photograph intentionally tossed, or was it lost? Is the trash more concentrated on certain blocks? The objects people leave behind can serve as unintentional, anonymous portraits. I started going on trash walks after discovering the work of Yuji Agematsu , a conceptual artist who makes daily assemblages out of urban debris he picks up. If you’re a germaphobe, you can use gloves or a grabber tool while on the trash walk. What you do with the pieces of garbage after — whether you turn them into sculptures, use them as inspiration for poetry or just toss them away in a bin — is entirely up to you. Fantastic! Thank you so much, Anna Kodé! And everyone: Look out for Anna’s book , and check out her newsletter . She’s a Hero of Noticing! Leave a comment More walk posts: BECOME A SUPPORTER Do you support this newsletter’s mission — to help us all stay human and engaged and creative and excited by life? Join the community of TAoN Supporters! You’ll get access to the full archives as well as Supporter-only posts and participatory threads. Your support makes this newsletter possible. Seriously. Thank you! Subscribe now THE NEXT FREE EDITION IN TWO WEEKS! IN THE MAIL I left out one item from my recent mailbox roundup the other day: a postcard for Joy Scavengers , a project I wasn’t familiar with. How it works: “Once a month, Joy Scavengers sends you a free physical or digital postcard with seven ordinary things to look for .” That’s it! Example above. I love the range of items/incidents to look out for listed on the postcard. ( Notable that one is “someone picking up litter.” ) You can sign up here . The site also includes Q&As with artist/writer “scavengers,” pictures submitted by participants, and more. Lovely project! IN OTHER NEWS For Fast Company , I wrote about the return of designer Tibor Kalman’s watches that amusingly subvert what a timepiece can be . The Oakland Noticing Club notices things happening in the background. Speaking of trash : fascinating Odd Lots episode on NYC garbage management. Write a tanka : a 31-syllable Japanese form that “is like a haiku-plus .” Why old-line law firms are called “white shoe” firms . Soviet-era anti-drinking posters. The visual communication of Otto Neurath . “ Draw a horse , then let it run across the gradient screen and make friends.” — Swiss-Miss . Mason Currey is planning a series on How To Try Hard in Writing and Art. New Orleans’ tiniest art gallery is now located in a brick wall outside The Elysian Bar , 2317 Burgundy St. Fun project! OKAY THAT’S IT! As always, I value your feedback (suggestions, critiques, positive reinforcement, constructive insults directed at me, not at anyone else , etc.), as well as your tips or stories or personal noticing rituals, things we need a word for, and of course your icebreakers : consumed@robwalker.net. Or use the comments. —> Or just click the heart symbol. That always makes my day. wild.title: In the Mail
wild.description: Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for November is BROKEN. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! Hi all, It’s been a little while since I shared some of what has arrived in my (physical) mailbox. But today I’m inspired by some very impressive (and generous) mail from the ever-productive Kevin Kelly . Kelly’s new Design Prompts is a nifty box of 110 double-sided cards with prompts to “help creative people get unstuck.” It’s inspired by Brian Eno’s famous Oblique Strategies card deck, but these are Kevin’s own prompts, described as “more general purpose.” Random examples: Lean into extravagance Don’t play the hero Yes, then what? Fake it Employ the most retro idea Fun! I imagine it must have been satisfying to write these — makes me want to try my hand at aphoristic prompts (or assign students to do so). Also, the box is really nice: Its magnetic cover closes with a very satisfying snap. It’s a limited edition of 400, for sale on Amazon for $25. More info on Kevin’s site here . Thanks, Kevin! More Kevin Kelly on TAoN: MORE MAIL As you may know, I offer a free three-month sub to the Supporter edition of TAoN to any current free subscriber who sends me physical mail. Recent folks who took me up on that: I got this fun postcard promoting World Collage Day, along with some great music tips from Amy G of Nashville. But Amy, you didn’t tell me your email address! Send to consumed@robwalker.net for comp sub. Read more
